Silicate–Melt Equilibria and the Phase Rule

Dr. Ahmad Redaa

26-10-2025

Why equilibrium matters in petrology

  • Magmas crystallize; rocks melt and transform.
  • Which phases (minerals/liquid) appear depends on: Temperature T, Pressure P, Composition X.
  • Phase relations are our “maps” for igneous & metamorphic processes.

Core question: Which phases can coexist at given T–P–X?

What do we mean by phase and component?

  • Phase (P): physically distinct, mechanically separable part (e.g., crystal, melt, vapor).
  • Component (C): minimal set of chemical “ingredients” to describe all phases present.
  • System: the portion we’re studying (e.g., pure water, a basaltic melt).
Term Example (everyday) Example (petrology)
Phase ice / liquid / vapor olivine / melt / vapor
Component H₂O SiO₂, MgO, FeO, …
System a pot of water magma + crystals in a chamber

Warm-up system: Pure water (H₂O)

Boiling water system.

Source: VectorStock

C = 1 (one component), with possible phases: - Solid (ice) - Liquid (water) - Vapor (steam)

We’ll use water to see how equilibrium conditions are constrained.

The Gibbs Phase Rule

We’ll use the rule, not its derivation:

\[ F = C - P + 2 \]

  • F: degrees of freedom (independent variables you can change without changing the number of phases present).
  • For lab/diagram cases at constant P or constant T, we often use reduced forms later. For now, keep the general form.

For water (C = 1): \(F = 3 - P\).

Apply Phase Rule to water

Phases present P F = 3 − P Meaning (at equilibrium)
Ice or Liquid or Vapor 1 2 You can vary T and P independently and stay in that single-phase field.
Liquid + Vapor 2 1 You can vary one variable; the other is fixed by the boiling curve.
Ice + Liquid 2 1 Must stay on the melting/freezing curve.
Ice + Liquid + Vapor 3 0 Triple point: T and P fixed; any change loses a phase.

Phase regions vs. coexistence lines

Phase Diagram of Water.

Source: https://www.expii.com

  • Regions on T–P diagram = single phase (F = 2 for water).
  • Lines = two-phase equilibrium (F = 1).
  • Point where three lines meet = triple point (F = 0).

Takeaway from water

  • Equilibrium limits freedom: more coexisting phases → fewer degrees of freedom.
  • This logic directly transfers to minerals + melt in rocks.
  • Now, let’s scale up.

Unary system: SiO₂ polymorphs

SiO₂ equilibrium phase diagram.

Source: https://www.science.smith.edu

  • C = 1 (SiO₂) with multiple phases: quartz, tridymite, cristobalite (+ melt).
  • Each phase is stable over certain T–P ranges.
  • Triple point(s) where three phases coexist → F = 0.

Teaching points: - Same counting as water: 1 component, multiple phases. - Phase boundaries mark where one phase replaces another at equilibrium.

Binary systems: two components

NaAlSi₃O₈–CaAl₂Si₂O₈ equilibrium phase diagram.

Source: https://www.science.smith.edu

Example: Albite (Ab) – Anorthite (An) feldspar series
C = 2, phases can include melt and one or more solids.

Key diagram features to label: - Liquidus (start of crystallization)
- Solidus (end of crystallization)
- Two-phase region (solid + liquid) - Eutectic: invariant point where 2 solids + 1 liquid coexist (F = 0)

Reading a binary phase diagram (Ab–An)

NaAlSi₃O₈–CaAl₂Si₂O₈ equilibrium phase diagram.

Source: https://www.science.smith.edu

  1. Pick a bulk composition (x-axis).
  2. At a given T, draw a horizontal line:
    • If above liquidus → melt only (P = 1 → F = 2 − 1 + 2? Careful: here we treat T, composition axes; conceptually: single phase).
    • Between liquidus & solidus → melt + crystals (P = 2 → F = 1 along that tie-line).
    • Below solidus → solid assemblage.
  3. Cooling path follows the liquidus down to eutectic; at eutectic, both solids crystallize together.

Phase rule insight on binary eutectic

At the eutectic (isobaric, isothermal diagram section): - Coexisting phases: Solid A + Solid B + Liquid → \(P = 3\) - Components: C = 2 - At variable T and composition axes (P held fixed in lab), the eutectic is invariant → effectively no freedom: fixed T and composition of liquid and solids at that point.

Intuition: maximum coexistence = minimum freedom.

Petrological meaning (binary)

  • Crystallization sequence: which phase appears first depends on bulk composition and liquidus shape.
  • Fractional crystallization: early crystals remove elements from melt → melt composition evolves.
  • Natural link: explains why basaltic magmas can differentiate into diverse rock types.

Ternary systems: three components

CaMgSi₂O₆–Mg₂SiO₄–CaAl₂Si₂O₈ diagram.

Source: Smith College Petrology Resources

Example (basalt analog): Diopside–Anorthite–Forsterite (Di–An–Fo)
- C = 3, phases include melt and one or more solids. - Plot on a triangle: each vertex = 100% of one component; any point inside = mixture.

Key features: - Cotectic lines: melt coexists with two solids.
- Ternary eutectic (invariant trough point): melt + three solids.

Following paths on a ternary diagram

  • Start with bulk melt composition (a point in the triangle).
  • On cooling, composition of the residual melt travels along liquid paths toward cotectics.
  • Where three solids and melt meet → ternary eutectic (invariant).

Practice prompt (in-class): mark a starting melt and sketch its liquid line of descent to the eutectic.

Comparing systems: same logic, growing complexity

System C Typical phases Special invariant
Water 1 ice / liquid / vapor Triple point (P = 3 → F = 0)
SiO₂ 1 quartz / tridymite / cristobalite / melt Triple points among polymorphs
Ab–An 2 plagioclase(s), melt Eutectic (2 solids + liquid)
Di–An–Fo 3 pyroxene/olivine/plagioclase + melt Ternary eutectic (3 solids + liquid)

The phase rule constrains all of them.
